facts: Barbaresco is made from the Nebbiolo grape and became a DOCG in 1980, after DOC status in 1966.
DOCG rules require a minimum of 2 years ageing before release, with at least 9 months in wooden barrels, and at least 4 years for riserva.
The minimum alcohol level is 12.5 per cent, though most wines are closer to 13.5 per cent.
Barbaresco is allowed to age a year less than Barolo, and its tannins tend to soften more quickly.
The Barbaresco Consorzio introduced Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive (MEGA) subzones in 2007, and the final number of subzones is 66.
Barolo is a red DOCG wine made from the Nebbiolo grape, and the zone was raised to DOCG status in 1980.
A Barolo must be aged at least three years, a minimum of 38 months from November 1 of the harvest year, with at least 18 months in wooden barrels.
Barolo Riserva requires five years of total ageing, a minimum of 62 months from November 1 of the harvest year, with at least 18 months in barrel.
Over 87% of Barolo comes from the communes of Barolo, La Morra, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba.
In 2010 the Barolo Consorzio introduced MGA subzones, with 181 delimited, of which 170 are vineyard areas and 11 are village designations.
Brunello di Montalcino is made 100% from Sangiovese, and in 1980 it was one of the first four wines awarded DOCG status.
The current ageing rules, set in 1998, require 2 years in oak and at least 4 months in bottle, with Normale released 50 months after harvest and Riserva a year later.
Montalcino has one of the warmest and driest climates in Tuscany, with average annual rainfall of around 28 inches, compared with 35 inches in Chianti.
Producers can also make Sant'Antimo DOC wines, which allow grapes other than Sangiovese, and the sweet white Moscadello di Montalcino from Muscat.
Chianti Classico is a Tuscan DOCG made from 80 to 100% Sangiovese, with other red grapes allowed up to a maximum of 20%.
Chianti Classico became its own denomination in 1996 and is no longer a subzone of Chianti.
The symbol of the Lega del Chianti, a black rooster on a gold field, became the emblem of the Chianti Classico consortium.
Riserva needs at least two years of ageing, including at least three months in bottle, and a minimum total alcohol of 12.5%.
Etna became a DOC in 1968, the first DOC of Sicily and one of the oldest in Italy.
Etna Rosso and Rosato require at least 80% Nerello Mascalese, with Nerello Cappuccio making up no more than 20%.
Etna Bianco requires at least 60% Carricante, and Bianco Superiore requires at least 80% Carricante with grapes coming only from the Milo area.
The soil is volcanic, rocky, fast-draining and rich in minerals, formed from decomposed lava, ash and sand.
Vineyard altitude varies between about 1,475 and 3,610 feet, which causes large temperature differences between day and night and across the seasons.
Barbera is the most widely planted grape, with Nebbiolo and Dolcetto also significant for red wine, and Moscato leading among whites.
Barolo and Barbaresco are both made from Nebbiolo, and Nebbiolo takes its name from the Piedmontese word nebia, meaning fog.
The Barbaresco DOCG requires a minimum alcohol of 12.5% and 2 years minimum ageing, or 4 years for riserva.
The region has no IGT classification, and about 90% of winemaking takes place in the south around Alba, Asti and Alessandria.
Prosecco is made from the Glera grape, renamed in Italy in 2009, and the rules allow up to 15% of other permitted varieties.
Since 1 January 2010, Prosecco is exclusively a geographical indication and no longer the name of a grape variety.
Prosecco is usually made by the Charmat-Martinotti method, with secondary fermentation in large stainless steel tanks and a minimum production time of 30 days.
Most Prosecco DOC is made as spumante or frizzante, and only about 5% is still tranquillo wine.
Brut has up to 12 grams per litre of residual sugar, Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/L and Dry has 17 to 32 g/L.
Garganega is the principal grape, and Soave must contain a minimum of 70% Garganega.
Soave Superiore has been a DOCG since 2001, created for the 2002 vintage, and Recioto di Soave received its own DOCG in 1998.
Soave Classico comes from hillside vineyards around Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone, with limestone soils in the west and decomposed volcanic rock in the east.
Recioto di Soave uses the appassimento drying process and keeps much of its sweetness.
Soave Superiore Riserva needs a minimum alcohol of 12.5% and at least 24 months of ageing, with at least three months in bottle.
Taurasi is a red wine from the province of Avellino in Campania, made principally from Aglianico, and it became a DOCG in 1993.
Under DOCG rules Taurasi must be aged at least 3 years before release, with at least 1 year in wood, and Riserva at least 4 years.
Up to 15% of Barbera, Piedirosso and Sangiovese may be blended with the Aglianico.
The vineyards sit on volcanic soil, and Aglianico thrives at altitudes of around 1,300 to 1,600 feet above sea level.
Valpolicella is a DOC red wine from the province of Verona, authorized in 1968, blended mainly from Corvina and/or Corvinone at 45 to 95% and Rondinella at 5 to 30%.
Classico comes from the original zone around Negrar, Marano di Valpolicella, Fumane, Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella and San Pietro in Cariano, and Valpantena comes from the Valpantena valley.
Ripasso wine is passed over the pressed skins of Recioto or Amarone before barrel ageing, which gives it more body, flavor and alcohol.
Valpolicella Ripasso is a DOC of its own, and Amarone and Recioto della Valpolicella, made from partly dried grapes, are DOCGs of their own.
It is the only true continental climate zone in New Zealand, with large daily and seasonal temperature extremes, protected from the maritime climate by high mountains.
Frost can occur at any time between March and November, and heavy frosts are common throughout winter.
The harvest begins in mid to late April, some six to seven weeks later than in the more northerly vineyards.
Soils are rough-edged mica and other metamorphic schists in silt loams that drain easily, so irrigation is generally essential.
The sub-regions include Bannockburn, Bendigo, Tarras, Gibbston, Wānaka, Alexandra Basin and Cromwell Basin, with Gibbston the coolest and highest.
Marlborough is by far New Zealand's largest wine region, with three quarters of the country's wine production and 70% of its vineyard area in 2020.
Marlborough was registered as a Geographical Indication in 2018, and its Sauvignon Blanc is recognised as world class.
The Wairau Valley soils are primarily free-draining alluvial gravels, and cool night-time sea breezes give the temperature variation needed for good wines.
The three sub-regions are the Wairau Valley, the Southern Valleys with largely glacial loess soils, and the cooler Awatere Valley.
Méthode Marlborough wines must be made entirely in Marlborough by the traditional method and aged on lees for a minimum of 18 months.
Appellation Marlborough Wine requires wines to be made entirely from sustainably grown Marlborough grapes and bottled in New Zealand.
Portugal has two UNESCO World Heritage wine regions, the Douro Valley and Pico Island.
Bairrada is named for the Portuguese word barro, meaning clay, and its main grape is Baga.
Port needs schist-rich soil in the Douro Valley, and Portugal has many native grapes, including Touriga Nacional in the Douro and Dão.
